terms.definition: Slow down and stop if needed to let priority traffic pass safely.
The side of the road or vehicle closest to the kerb. In the UK this is the left side.
The side of the vehicle closest to the centre of the road. In the UK this is the right side.
A road with a central barrier or reservation separating opposite directions of traffic.
A road with no central reservation between opposite traffic lanes.
The default upper speed limit for a road type when no number is shown. For cars it is 60 mph on single carriageways and 70 mph on dual carriageways.
An area with street lights, usually with a 30 mph limit in England and Scotland. In Wales the default limit is 20 mph.
A low-speed area near homes, shops, or schools to protect people walking and cycling.
A signed speed limit often used on wider urban main roads.
White or yellow zig-zag lines near crossings or schools. Do not park there or overtake near a crossing.
A yellow criss-cross grid painted at busy junctions. Do not enter unless your exit is clear.
A box at traffic lights marked with a bike symbol for cyclists to wait ahead. Cars stop at the first white line on red or amber.
Short for advanced stop line, a waiting box for cyclists at traffic lights.
A green arrow light allowing traffic to turn only in the arrow direction.
The emergency strip on the left side of a motorway. Use it only in emergencies or when gantry signs show a speed limit above it.
An overhead motorway signal showing a lane is closed ahead. Move to an open lane safely.
A crossing with black and white stripes and flashing orange beacons. Give way to anyone waiting and stop once someone steps onto it.
A signal-controlled crossing with a flashing amber phase after red. During flashing amber, give way to anyone still crossing.
A smart signal-controlled crossing that senses people crossing. It goes straight from red and amber to green with no flashing amber.
A wide signal-controlled crossing shared by pedestrians and cyclists. Follow the traffic lights as at a puffin crossing.
A small junction with a painted white circle in the centre. Drive around the circle and give way to the right.
Mirrors, Signal, Manoeuvre: the routine for changing speed, position, or direction safely.
The area beside and behind your car that your mirrors cannot show. Look over your shoulder before moving off or changing lanes.
Pedestrian priority rule at junctions. Give way to people crossing or waiting to cross a side road.
Hierarchy of road users. Drivers of larger vehicles carry greater responsibility to reduce danger.
Priority for cyclists and horse riders. Do not cut across them when turning or changing lanes.
The United Kingdom. Traffic drives on the left.
Great Britain: England, Scotland, and Wales.
Approved Driving Instructor, qualified to teach learners including on motorways in dual-control cars.
Emergency telephone marker on motorways and in emergency areas.
A circular junction where UK traffic travels clockwise around a central island.
A short lane used to join or leave a motorway or dual carriageway.
The strip or barrier dividing opposite traffic carriageways.
A solid white line across your lane. Stop behind it for red lights or Stop signs.
A check for safe following distance. Count two seconds after the car ahead passes a marker.
A lane marked for buses, cycles, and taxis. Check the sign for its active hours.
A marked lane for pedal cycles on the road. A solid white line keeps cars out during its hours.
An orange bay with an SOS phone on motorways without a hard shoulder.
A road where stopping is not allowed on the main carriageway.
Roadworks layout where traffic temporarily shares the opposite carriageway in narrow lanes.
The time gap between your front bumper and the vehicle ahead.
An overhead bridge carrying lane signals and variable speed limits above a motorway.
